extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, literary-criticism students, and readers of classical poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative rules (from Aristotle/translator's preface and contents) for composing and judging poetry in its major forms—especially tragedy and epic—covering aims, parts, plot structure, diction, and staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as Imitation (Mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: All the different sorts of Poetry are only Imitations (mimesis); poetry imitates life by means of number, discourse, and harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poetry as an imitative art: understand what is being imitated (actions, characters, manners) and with what means (rhythm/number, language/discourse, music/harmony). The analogy to painting and to musical arts is used to clarify how imitation operates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of Imitation — Number, Discourse, Harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: The arts employ three means to imitate: (1) number, (2) discourse, and (3) harmony (music). Different poetic forms use these in different combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: flute/harp use number and harmony; dancers use number; epopeia/epic uses primarily discourse (prose or verse); tragedy and comedy employ combinations of the three. Choosing and balancing the means is essential to form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive Species: epic (epopæia), tragedy, comedy, dithyrambic
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic forms are different species within the genus 'poetry'—they differ in the means they employ, the subjects they treat, and the manner of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating, identify the genre and apply the appropriate rules: e.g., epic differs from tragedy in subject-treatment and allowable length; dithyrambics and other forms have particular uses of music and chorus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of actions, and not of Men nor their Manners; it has six parts and its proper object is action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on constructing a coherent action (plot) rather than merely portraying character traits or moral qualities; the fable/plot is the essential backbone of a tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose/Effect of Tragedy — arouse pity and fear (catharsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of Tragedy is to move the passions—specifically to excite terror and pity—and thereby refine or purge the passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose incidents and episodes so they naturally produce pity and fear in the audience; plot devices should be chosen to achieve this emotional and moral effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Six Parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is composed of six parts: (1) Plot (fable), (2) Character (manners), (3) Thought, (4) Diction, (5) Melody, (6) Spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority: Plot is the most important, then character; diction, thought, melody, and spectacle follow. Evaluate or craft each part and how it serves the whole; do not mistake spectacle for the essence of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and Integrity of Action (Unity of the Subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must be a whole with a beginning, middle, and end; the action must be single and complete, with all parts connected and necessary to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extraneous episodes and digressions. Ensure causal and logical linkage among incidents so the action reads as one integrated whole of proper extent for representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot Structure: Peripeteia (Reversal) and Anagnorisis (Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex plots use peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition/memory) under certain conditions; these are powerful devices when properly combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peripeteia and recognition should be single, well-conditioned, and produce surprise fitting the plot; their arrangement must be probable and causally motivated to provoke pity and fear effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex Fable (Plot Types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots divide into simple (without reversal/recognition) and complex (with reversal/recognition); the complex plot is often superior when its components are apt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose plot type based on desired emotional effect; complex plots that produce surprise and are causally convincing often produce stronger tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Nature and Management of Character
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters (manners) chosen for tragedy should be appropriate to the action: considerations include simplicity vs complexity, moral quality, consistency, and whether the catastrophe is happy or fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be consistent and believable within the action. A tragic protagonist typically is neither wholly good nor wholly bad; their traits must contribute to and be revealed through the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terrible and Pitiful Incidents — Causes and Appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: What makes incidents terrible or pitiful depends on their causal structure and the poet's management; monstrous or purely decorative incidents are erroneous means to these ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid provoking terror or pity via gratuitous decoration or monstrous, causeless incidents. Prefer incidents that arise naturally from character and necessity; three sorts of cruel actions are distinguished and judged for suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude (Probability) vs Strict Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets may prefer verisimilitude (what seems probable) to literal truth; what is plausible to the audience can be preferred to actual fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When truth cannot be followed without harm to the poetic effect, prefer the probable or plausible. Still, preserve causal explanation and intelligibility; disguise or justify extraordinary elements when admitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent/Length of Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are bounds to the length of dramatic pieces and different bounds for epic; tragedy should have a single action of a suitable length for representation, while epic may be longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a tragedy within limits that allow coherent representation from beginning to end; epic can be more extensive but must still retain unity and causality appropriate to its form.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Chorus: its Role and Proper Use
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus is an essential part of tragedy and has defined functions (songs, motions); its songs and interpositions must be appropriate, not foreign or vitious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Chorus to support the action and emotional effect rather than distract; avoid foreign songs or strange introductions that impair unity or verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction, Figures, and Ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear and noble expression is required; barbarisms, enigma, and frivolous ornamentation are faults; the ornaments of speech are valuable but vicious if overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for clarity and nobility in diction; use metaphors and figured words with restraint and purpose. Evaluate diction both for appropriateness to character and for its contribution to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of Tragic Rules to Epic Poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of tragedy apply to epic with necessary adjustments: epic shares many parts with tragedy but differs in length, verse, and certain liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting tragic principles to epic, allow epic's greater scope (longer extent, different verse), but maintain unity of action, causality of incidents, and appropriate ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality Requirement for Incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: All incidents in a poem ought to have causes and reasons; incidents without cause should be avoided except in limited, justified cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every incident either follows from prior events or is plausibly motivated; if an impossible or unlikely incident is introduced, disguise or justify it within the poem's internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for the Unravelling (Denouement) and Use of Machines
rubrics_metrics.description: There are strictures about how the unraveling (unravelling) of the plot should occur and when mechanical devices (machines/deus ex machina) may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer natural, causally-motivated unravelings; allow machines only when they do not vitiate the unity and probability of the plot and when permitted by the nature of the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Practice and Genius; Limits of Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules cannot give genius; they only show the path a genius ought to tread; precepts alone are insufficient without meditation and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rules as guides to train judgment and craft; cultivate practice and study of exemplary poems (ancient poems) to gain true insight rather than relying on rules alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Criticism — discover virtues and vices
rubrics_metrics.description: Good criticism should discover and mark exactly the virtues and vices of a work rather than merely flatter; one should point out faults to discover truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should balance respect for greatness with frank identification of defects, explaining causes and offering corrections where appropriate. Avoid censoriousness aimed merely at decrying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division and Classification of Ornaments of Discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornaments of speech (figures, metaphors, etc.) are divisible and have appropriate places; excessive use makes them vicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify rhetorical ornaments and deploy them suitably to different parts of a poem; reserve strong ornamentation for passages that demand it and avoid trivial or repetitive embellishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and Scope of Comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is defined with respect to ridicule and its objects; its origin, development, and why it was cultivated later than tragedy are discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or judging comedy, consider how ridicule functions, who the targets are, and how chorus, drums, and public taste shape comedic practice; apply genre-specific rules distinct from tragedy.
